analysis.title: U.S. midterms: Ten questions investors should be asking (CIO Special)
key_insights: Predicting the midterm result correctly does not guarantee the right portfolio decision. What matters is how the outcome compares with what the market has already priced in.

Current forecasts favor Democrats taking control of the House, though surprises remain possible. The 2016 presidential election is the reference case: markets fell initially on Trump's surprise win, then the decline more than reversed by the end of the next trading day.

Some of the biggest surprises could come from state and local races. Governors, state legislators and local officials influence electricity supply, transmission lines, planning decisions and data center permits, so a result that barely moves a broad index could still matter for individual companies awaiting project approvals.

The president's party has usually lost House seats at midterms and 2026 looks consistent with that. Trump is serving a second, non-consecutive term, which is rare (only Grover Cleveland before). Second-term consecutive presidents are the closer modern parallel and show a stronger 'six-year itch' effect.
U.S. equities have often weakened ahead of midterms and recovered afterwards, but this describes what happened, not why, so DWS treats it as a reference point rather than a prediction.

Divided government is not necessarily good for markets. Cited research finds higher average excess equity returns under unified than divided government. Fewer laws do not mean less uncertainty, since annual spending bills still raise the risk of funding disputes and a government shutdown.

Election results can turn AI infrastructure politics into an earnings issue. Local legislators could scrutinize data center permits, ask developers to contribute more to infrastructure or protect households from rising power costs. Broader AI productivity gains could matter more for equity valuations than the data center debate.

Gridlock does not mean fiscal discipline. Existing federal spending continues, interest costs accumulate, and annual funding compromises could preserve or add spending. For Treasuries the question is deficits, debt issuance and the yields required to attract buyers.

First election-night results should be treated with caution. If Senate control hinges on one or two close races, the apparent outcome can change with late ballots, recounts, litigation and differing state certification. Equities, rates, oil and the dollar can move as the perceived probability of an outcome changes.

DWS expects politics to return to business as usual for markets. There is less at stake at midterms than in presidential elections, and even Senate control coming down to one seat would have limited investment implications. Investors should focus on decisions newly elected officials promise rather than who won.

For equities, the S&P 500 has typically been weak in the months before midterms and recovered in the following year, but 12-month returns after individual midterms vary considerably. Under Republican presidents since 1953 (small samples), average annual S&P 500 returns were positive for every combination of congressional control, but much higher when Republicans controlled at least one chamber than when Democrats held both the House and Senate.

Party control alone is a poor investment signal. Earnings, productivity, monetary policy and valuations likely matter more, though effects could be larger for individual companies and sectors if the result changes tariffs, regulation or the political environment around AI infrastructure.

For bonds, the implications may emerge gradually. Political uncertainty can affect the extra compensation investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds, so the focus is on whether the policy mix changes the expected path of inflation, Treasury yields and long-term debt prices.

In credit, across the six midterms since 2002 with Bloomberg Global high-yield spread data, election outcomes show little consistent independent effect on spreads. Post-election moves tracked the credit cycle and macro events: the second round of QE in 2010, the 2014 oil shock and Fed tightening in 2018.

sector_views.rationale: State and local election outcomes could tighten permitting or shift infrastructure costs onto developers, creating earnings risk for some AI buildout beneficiaries. Broader AI productivity gains could outweigh this.

risk_factors: Recounts, litigation and late-counted ballots in tight races could change the apparent Senate outcome after election night.
State and local regulation of AI infrastructure and data center permitting.
Government funding disputes and a possible shutdown under divided government.
Deficits, debt issuance and higher term premium on Treasuries.
Changes to tariffs, fiscal policy and regulation affecting company and sector earnings.
vol_and_positioning: Equities, interest rates, oil and the U.S. dollar can move as the perceived probability of a political outcome changes, including on election night before final results.
geopolitical: U.S. midterm elections on 3 November 2026: all 435 House seats, 35 Senate races including two special elections, and 39 state and territorial governorships
Tariff policy could change depending on the election result
Possible government shutdown from disputes over annual spending bills under divided government

tension_points.bull_case: Conventional Wall Street thinking sees gridlock as positive because it makes major legislative change harder.
tension_points.bear_case: Research finds higher average excess equity returns under unified than divided government, and gridlock still leaves shutdown risk and unresolved fiscal arithmetic.

theme_stances.key_argument: Party control alone is a poor investment signal, and politics should return to business as usual for markets.
theme_stances.evidence: party control alone is a poor investment signal

theme_stances.evidence: politics into an earnings issue for some beneficiaries of the AI buildout
